title: Electrolysis
learningObjective: Understand why covalent compounds do not conduct electricity; Understand why ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or in aqueous solution; Know that anion and cation are terms used to refer to negative and positive ions, respectively; Describe experiments to investigate electrolysis, using inert electrodes, of molten compounds (including lead(II) bromide) and aqueous solutions (including sodium chloride, dilute sulfuric acid and copper(II) sulfate) and to predict the products; Write ionic half-equations representing the reactions at the electrodes during electrolysis and understand why these reactions are classified as oxidation or reduction; Practical: Investigate the electrolysis of aqueous solutions

sections.title: Electrolysis — the chapter map
sections.markdown:
Connect a piece of copper to a battery and a complete circuit: the copper
warms up slightly, and nothing else happens. Connect a solution of potassium
iodide into the same kind of circuit instead, and something genuinely new
occurs — a chemical change. Bubbles of hydrogen gas appear at one electrode,
purple iodine is produced at the other, and neither substance was there
before. That contrast is the whole business of this chapter: electricity
passing through some substances just makes them warm, while electricity
passing through others **tears them apart into new substances**. The process
that does the tearing is **electrolysis**, and by the end of the lesson you
will be able to predict its products for any compound the exam throws at you.

Every objective of record for this lesson is a **chemistry-only**
specification statement — assessed in **Paper 2 (2C) only**; none of them
appears on Paper 1 (1C), and none is shared with Science Double Award:

- understand why **covalent compounds do not conduct** electricity
  (spec 1.55C);
- understand why **ionic compounds conduct only when molten or in aqueous
  solution** (spec 1.56C);
- know that **anion** and **cation** name negative and positive ions
  respectively (spec 1.57C);
- **describe experiments** to investigate electrolysis, using inert
  electrodes, of molten compounds (including lead(II) bromide) and aqueous
  solutions (including sodium chloride, dilute sulfuric acid and copper(II)
  sulfate) — and **predict the products** (spec 1.58C);
- **write ionic half-equations** for the electrode reactions and classify
  them as oxidation or reduction (spec 1.59C);
- **practical**: investigate the electrolysis of aqueous solutions
  (spec 1.60C).

The lesson runs in four movements after this map. First, the conduction
rulebook — which structures carry a current and which refuse, and why, ending
in the definitions of electrolysis itself and the apparatus it needs. Second,
the molten-compound case study: molten lead(II) bromide, every observation
explained, and the redox language (oxidation, reduction, OILRIG) that grades
the reactions at the two electrodes. Third, the aqueous case studies — sodium
chloride, copper(II) sulfate and dilute sulfuric acid solutions — where water
itself joins the competition and changes the products, closing with the
prediction rules that work for every solution. Fourth, the quantitative
experiment: measuring how the volume of gas produced depends on the current,
and reading a proportional relationship off a graph. Work through the
sections in order — each movement's equipment feeds directly into the next.

:::prior-knowledge
Four pieces of earlier work carry this lesson. **Ionic bonding** from
Chapter 7 (u1:c07) — ionic compounds are lattices of positive and negative
ions, and in the solid state those ions are locked in place. **Covalent
bonding** from Chapter 8 (u1:c08) — covalent molecular substances are made of
individual molecules with their electrons held tightly in atoms and bonds.
**Metallic bonding** from Chapter 9 (u1:c09) — metals conduct because
delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice. **Charges and
formulae** from Chapters 5 and 6 — you must write ion charges instantly
(Pb²⁺, Br⁻, Al³⁺, O²⁻), because half-equations are charge bookkeeping.
:::

:::exam-hint
Everything here is chemistry-only: Paper 2C territory, never Paper 1C, and
Double Award candidates can set the chapter aside. The question shapes are
extremely predictable: state the products at each electrode; explain why the
solid did not conduct but the melt did; write and balance a half-equation and
label it oxidation or reduction; predict products for an unfamiliar solution
from the reactivity rules; and describe or interpret the quantitative
experiment. Learn the half-equations as a fixed set and the prediction rules
as two sentences — the marks follow mechanically.
:::

:::misconception
"Passing electricity through any substance causes a chemical change." The
copper wire at the start of this section is the standing counterexample: it
conducts, it warms, and **nothing new is made**, because conduction in a metal
is electrons drifting through a structure that stays intact. A chemical change
needs a structure that is **broken apart by the process** — that requires
mobile **ions**, and only molten or dissolved ionic compounds (plus a few
covalent exceptions) offer them. Conduction and decomposition are different
events; this chapter is about the second.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.55C–1.60C items across the whole lesson — the
chemistry-only badge, the conduction rules, the prediction set and the
half-equation bank. If you can already say why the potassium iodide solution
produced new substances while the copper wire produced none — charged
particles, free to move, then pulled apart at the electrodes — the movements
ahead will slot straight into place.
:::

sections.title: Why things conduct electricity
sections.markdown:
One rule runs every conduction question in this course: **for a substance to
conduct electricity it must contain charged particles, and those charged
particles must be free to move.** Both conditions matter. Charged but
immobile conducts nothing; mobile but neutral conducts nothing either. The
charged particles are always one of two kinds — **electrons** or **ions** —
and the first thing to decide in any conduction question is which of the two
is doing the moving in the structure in front of you.

**Metals** conduct because the moving particles are electrons. The metal
structure is a [[lattice]] of positive ions surrounded by a sea of
[[delocalised-electron]]s, and those delocalised electrons are free to move
throughout the whole structure — that is why a solid metal wire carries a
current with no fuss and no chemical change. **Ionic compounds** behave
completely differently. In the **solid** state their ions are held tightly in
position in the lattice — they can vibrate on the spot, but they cannot leave
their lattice positions — so although charged particles are present, they are
not free to move, and the solid does not conduct. **Melt** the compound, or
**dissolve** it in water, and the ions break loose: now they are free to move
around, and the molten liquid or aqueous solution conducts. The ions do not
drift aimlessly, though — under the pull of a power supply they move
purposefully towards the electrodes, and that purposeful movement is exactly
what makes the next section's chemical changes possible.

That mobility story is also where the two ion names come from, and both names
must be used precisely:

- **[[anion]]** — a **negative** ion (think *A* for the *A*-minus charge:
  anions crawl to the positive electrode);
- **[[cation]]** — a **positive** ion.

Where each name comes from — the electrodes themselves — is a story the
lesson returns to once the electrodes have been introduced properly.

**Covalent molecular substances** are the third structure type, and they are
the refuseniks. Substances such as methane (CH₄), carbon dioxide (CO₂) and
hexane consist of **individual molecules** with no overall electrical charge
and no ions anywhere: every electron is held tightly either in an atom or in
a covalent bond between atoms, and none can move from molecule to molecule.
No charged particles, no movement, no conduction — **in any state, solid,
liquid or gas, and in solution too**. That triple refusal is what spec 1.55C
asks you to explain, and the explanation is always the same two-clause
sentence: molecules carry no overall charge, and the electrons are not free
to move.

There is one honest crack in the covalent wall, and examiners love it. A few
covalent substances **react with water to form ions**, and once ions exist,
the solution conducts. Ammonia dissolves in water to give a solution
containing ammonium ions and hydroxide ions. Hydrogen chloride gas dissolves
in water to form hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq), in which the HCl has ionised.
The conduction there is real — but it is ionic conduction borrowed through a
chemical reaction with water, not molecular conduction. The molecules
themselves never conducted anything.

:::key-point
The conduction rulebook in one box. **Metals**: conduct solid and molten —
delocalised electrons are the mobile charge carriers. **Ionic compounds**:
do not conduct solid (ions locked in the lattice); conduct when **molten or
in aqueous solution** (ions free to move). **Covalent molecular compounds**:
never conduct — molecules are uncharged and the electrons are locked in atoms
and bonds — except when they react with water to make ions (ammonia solution,
hydrochloric acid). Say *which* particle moves in every answer: electrons
there, ions here.
:::

:::exam-hint
The classic question hands you a table of substances and states — solid
sodium chloride, molten sodium chloride, solid copper, aqueous copper(II)
sulfate — and asks which conduct. Answer with the rulebook, and always name
the mobile particle: solid ionic does not conduct because "the ions are held
in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move"; molten or aqueous does
because "the ions are free to move". Covalent molecular never conducts
because "there are no charged particles — the molecules are neutral and the
electrons are held in atoms and bonds". Presence of ions is not enough:
**mobility** is the mark-winning word.
:::

:::misconception
"Solid sodium chloride conducts because it is full of ions." It is indeed
full of ions — and it still does not conduct, because every one of those ions
is locked into its lattice position and can only vibrate on the spot. The
conduction rule needs charged particles **and** freedom to move, and the
solid state fails the second condition. Melting or dissolving is what buys
the freedom. Learners who write only "it has ions" for the solid case lose
the mark every time; write "ions present but not free to move" and the mark
is yours.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.55C/1.56C/1.57C items — the conduction table for
the three structure types, the solid-vs-molten/aqueous contrast, and the
anion/cation vocabulary. Drill the two-clause covalent explanation and the
mobility half of the ionic story until both are word-perfect; every later
section in this lesson leans on them.
:::

sections.title: Passing electricity through compounds: electrolysis
sections.markdown:
Pass a current through a metal and you observe almost nothing — the metal
gets slightly warmer, and that is all, because electrons drift through an
intact structure. Pass a current through an **ionic compound that is molten
or in solution** and you observe a great deal: bubbling at the electrodes,
metals appearing, colours forming — new substances being made. That chemical
change has a name and a definition worth memorising word-for-word, because it
is a one-mark banker in every paper it can appear in:

**[[electrolysis]] is a chemical change caused by passing an electric current
through a compound which is either molten or in solution.**

The word is worth taking apart, because it is its own explanation:
**electro**-lysis is literally "splitting by electricity". The current does
not merely flow through the compound — it decomposes it. The substance being
split is carried in the second definition: an **[[electrolyte]]** is a liquid
or solution that undergoes electrolysis. Every electrolyte contains **ions**,
and the movement of those ions is responsible for two things at once — the
conduction of the electricity and the chemical changes at the electrodes. One
particle population, two jobs.

The current is fed into and out of the electrolyte through two
**[[electrode]]**s. **Carbon (graphite) is the standard electrode material**
because it conducts electricity and is chemically fairly **inert** — an
[[inert-electrode]] does not react with the substances being
produced. Platinum is also inert and can replace carbon; various other
metals are sometimes used, and what happens when the electrode material is
*not* inert is a story told later in the lesson. The two electrodes take
their names from their signs, and these names are fixed vocabulary from here
to the end of the course:

- the **positive** electrode is the **[[anode]]**;
- the **negative** electrode is the **[[cathode]]**.

The apparatus for molten-compound electrolysis is deliberately simple, and
you must be able to describe and draw it (spec 1.58C). A heat-proof crucible
holds the solid ionic compound; two carbon electrodes dip into it, held by a
lid with holes; the electrodes connect through wires and a bulb (or ammeter)
to a power supply — a 6 volt battery or a power pack, and the voltage is not
critical. Heat the crucible with a Bunsen burner. The bulb is the
experiment's storyteller: it stays dark while the compound is solid, and
lights the moment the compound melts. Light bulb = complete circuit = mobile
ions = conduction — and, as the next section explains, much more than
conduction.

:::key-point
Keep the two circuits in your head as one loop with two different carriers.
**Outside** the electrolyte — wires, power pack, bulb, the electrodes
themselves — the current is carried by **electrons**. **Inside** the
electrolyte, electrons cannot swim; the current is carried by **ions**
crawling towards the electrodes. The handover happens at the electrode
surfaces, and that handover *is* the chemistry of electrolysis.
:::

:::exam-hint
Three definitions come up again and again, and each must be exact.
**Electrolysis**: a chemical change caused by passing an electric current
through a compound that is molten or in solution — the "molten or in
solution" clause is compulsory, because it is the condition for mobile ions.
**Electrolyte**: a liquid or solution that undergoes electrolysis — and it
must contain ions. **Electrodes**: the conductors (carbon or platinum are
the named examples) that carry the current into and out of the electrolyte.
And the sign-pair — anode positive, cathode negative — has its own
mnemonic, **PANiC**: **P**ositive **A**node, **N**egative (is) **C**athode.
Carry it for the rest of the course; the paired AN OX / RED CAT arrives in
section 6.
:::

:::misconception
"The power supply must be powerful to force electrolysis to happen — more
volts, more splitting." A 6 volt battery or a standard power pack does the
job, and the voltage is not critical; what matters is that the electrolyte
contains mobile ions to complete the circuit. Raise the voltage and you may
push more current through, but the *existence* of the chemical change
depends on the ions, not the punch of the supply. Answers that blame "weak
electricity" for a non-conducting solid have the physics backwards — it is
the locked lattice that breaks the circuit, not a feeble battery.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.56C/1.58C items — the electrolysis definition,
the electrolyte and electrode vocabulary, and the molten-compound apparatus
sketch. Draw the crucible-and-electrodes setup from memory with all four
labels (electrolyte, electrodes, power supply, bulb) and say what the bulb
tells you at each stage of heating.
:::

sections.title: Explaining what is happening
sections.markdown:
The bulb lights because a complete circuit exists — but the chemical change
happens at the two electrode surfaces, and this section is the manual for
what occurs there. Start with what the power supply does. It pumps electrons
around the external circuit: it pulls electrons out of one electrode and
pushes them onto the other. The electrode **stripped of electrons** becomes
**positive** — that is the anode. The electrode **loaded with extra
electrons** becomes **negative** — that is the cathode. The signs of the
electrodes are not painted on; the power supply creates them, and the ions in
the electrolyte respond instantly to the electric field between them.

Now the ions move. **Positive ions ([[cation]]s) are attracted to the
negative electrode — the cathode.** When a cation touches the cathode, it
picks up the electrons it is short of, straight off the electrode surface.
Losing its charge, it becomes a neutral atom: it is **[[discharge]]d**.
**Negative ions ([[anion]]s) are attracted to the positive electrode — the
anode.** When an anion arrives, its **extra** electron — the one that made
it negative — moves off the ion onto the electron-hungry anode. The ion is
discharged too, becoming a neutral atom. Discharge is the whole event: ions
arrive, electrons cross the electrode surface one way or the other, neutral
atoms form. Those atoms are the products — metals at the cathode, non-metals
at the anode — and for elements whose atoms pair into molecules (bromine,
chlorine, oxygen, hydrogen), the atoms then join up two by two.

Each electrode event is written as a **[[half-equation]]** — the equation
for one half of the overall redox story, one electrode at a time. The
notation rules are short and strict:

- electrons are written as **e⁻** and appear on **one side only** — a
  half-equation shows a single process, either electron **gain** or electron
  **loss**, never both;
- the species before and after are **ions and atoms**: Pb²⁺ → Pb, Br⁻ → Br,
  H⁺ → H — with state symbols added when the question asks;
- the equation must balance in **atoms** and in **charge**: the total charge
  on the left must equal the total charge on the right.

The charge-balance rule is what fixes how many electrons each half-equation
carries. An ion's charge tells you directly: a 2+ ion needs **2** electrons
on the right-hand side to reach neutral; a 1− ion sheds exactly **1**
electron; a 2− ion sheds **2**; a 3+ ion absorbs **3**. For molecular
products the electrons also make the *molecule* arithmetic come out — two
1− halide ions shed 2 electrons between them to make one halogen molecule —
and the lesson's case studies build every one of those equations in full.

Finally, the classification vocabulary that spec 1.59C hangs on these
equations. An event in which a species **gains** electrons is
**[[reduction]]** — that is the cathode's job, so *reduction always happens
at the cathode*. An event in which a species **loses** electrons is
**[[oxidation]]** — the anode's job, so *oxidation always happens at the
anode*. Every half-equation is therefore labelled one or the other, and the
overall electrolysis — loss and gain running together — is called redox, a
word the next section unpacks properly with the OILRIG mnemonic.

:::key-point
The electron ledger. **Cathode (−)**: cations arrive, **gain** electrons from
the electrode, become atoms — **reduction**. **Anode (+)**: anions arrive,
**lose** their extra electron to the electrode, become atoms — **oxidation**.
Electrons supplied to the cathode by the power supply are carried away from
the anode by the same supply: the ledger always balances, because every
electron gained at the cathode was lost at the anode.
:::

:::exam-hint
Half-equation marks are won and lost on two checks. **Electron count**: read
it off the ion charge — charge magnitude = number of electrons transferred.
**Charge balance**: total charge left = total charge right (Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻
carries total 0 on the left, matching neutral Pb on the right). Then label
the event: electrons on the **left** (gain) = reduction; electrons on the
**right** (loss) = oxidation. Practise saying the label out loud as part of
the answer — "reduction, because the lead ions gain electrons" — because the
label is often a separate mark from the equation itself.
:::

:::misconception
"A half-equation should show electrons on both sides, one entering and one
leaving — otherwise the electrons don't balance." No — a *half*-equation
deliberately shows **one electrode's half** of the story, so electrons enter
or leave exactly once. If electrons appear on both sides, you have written
two processes in one equation, and that is not a half-equation at all. The
full electron balance across electrolysis comes from *pairing* the two
half-equations — one reduction at the cathode, one oxidation at the anode —
which is why they are called halves.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.59C items — discharge at each electrode,
half-equation writing with the charge-balance check, and the
oxidation/reduction labels. Write the generic cathode half-equation for a 2+
metal ion and the anode half-equation for a 1− halide ion from memory, with
labels, before meeting the real case studies in the next section.
:::

sections.title: The electrolysis of molten compounds
sections.markdown:
Lead(II) bromide, PbBr₂, is the set-piece experiment of spec 1.58C, and every
observation in it is explained by one idea from section 2 — ions locked in a
solid, freed by melting. The experiment: carbon electrodes dip into solid
PbBr₂ in a crucible, wired through a bulb to a power supply, and a Bunsen
burner heats the crucible. **Nothing at all happens until the lead(II)
bromide melts.** The moment it melts, four things occur, and you should be
able to narrate them in order:

- **the bulb lights** — electrons are flowing round the external circuit, so
  the circuit is complete: mobile charge carriers now exist inside the
  crucible;
- **bubbling and brown vapour appear at the anode** — the positive electrode,
  connected to the positive terminal, gives off brown bromine gas;
- **metallic lead collects at the cathode** — the negative electrode shows
  nothing dramatic while running, but underneath it, silvery molten lead is
  found;
- **when heating stops and the PbBr₂ solidifies again, everything stops** —
  no more bubbling, the bulb goes out. Refreeze the ions into the lattice and
  the circuit dies.

The explanation runs straight off the ionic model. Solid PbBr₂ is a giant
lattice of Pb²⁺ and Br⁻ ions packed in regular rows — the ions are locked
tightly in place, so the solid does not conduct and nothing happens. Melting
frees the ions to move. The power supply then creates the electron imbalance
at the electrodes (section 4), and the two ion populations walk to their
doom.

**At the cathode (−):** the positive Pb²⁺ ions are attracted to it, and each
arriving ion picks up two electrons from the electrode surface. Neutral lead
atoms form, and being dense molten metal, they pool underneath the electrode:

Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb  *(reduction — gain of electrons)*

**At the anode (+):** the negative Br⁻ ions are attracted to it, and each
arriving ion's extra electron moves onto the electron-starved electrode.
Neutral bromine atoms form:

Br⁻ → Br + e⁻  *(oxidation — loss of electrons)*

The bromine atoms do not stay single. A bromine atom has only 7 outer-shell
electrons, so each one joins to a partner through a covalent bond, giving
both atoms a full outer shell of 8 — bromine molecules, Br₂:

2Br → Br₂, and the overall anode **[[half-equation]]** is  2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

The new electrons on the anode flow away through the external circuit — which
is precisely why the bulb lights. Electrons in the wire; ions in the melt;
handover at the surfaces.

Now the vocabulary discipline that examiners police. We say the ions are
**[[discharge]]d** at the electrodes — discharge means the ion either gives
up electron(s) to the electrode or receives electron(s) from it, losing its
charge and becoming an atom. And keep the species names straight: **bromide
ions** travel to the anode and are converted into **bromine molecules** —
"bromide" and "bromine" name different species (ion versus molecule), and
mixing them in a written answer is a mark silently dropped. The same
precision applies at the cathode: lead ions are reduced to lead atoms.

:::key-point
Two carriers, one loop — the sentence examiners want for the bulb:
**electrons flow in the external circuit** (wire, power pack, bulb and the
electrode surfaces themselves), while **ions flow in the electrolyte** (the
molten compound). Neither carrier can cross the electrolyte; the electron
bookkeeping is completed by the discharge reactions at the two electrode
surfaces. Solid electrolyte = locked ions = no carriers = dark bulb.
:::

:::exam-hint
The lead(II) bromide question is a chain, and each link is its own mark:
(1) *why nothing happens while solid* — ions are held in fixed positions in
the lattice, not free to move; (2) *why the bulb lights on melting* — ions
become free to move and carry charge through the electrolyte, completing the
circuit; (3) *products* — bromine at the anode, lead at the cathode, each
with its half-equation; (4) *why it stops on cooling* — the ions return to
fixed lattice positions. Learn the chain as a script; the half-equations are
the two you met in section 4 with real species.
:::

:::misconception
"The lead forms at the anode because lead is dense and sinks to the bottom
where the anode is." Product placement is decided by **charge, not density**:
positive lead(II) ions are pulled to the negative cathode, where they gain
electrons and become lead atoms. Density only explains *where the lead
collects* (underneath the cathode, as molten metal pools), never *which
electrode it forms at*. Pair every product with its ion's charge — positive
ion → cathode, negative ion → anode — and placement errors disappear.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.58C/1.59C items — the molten lead(II) bromide
observation chain and the two half-equations with labels. Write both
half-equations from memory with the oxidation/reduction tags, then explain
in one sentence each why the bulb lights and why everything stops when the
melt freezes.
:::

sections.title: Electrolysis and redox
sections.markdown:
Look again at the two lead(II) bromide half-equations and classify them by
the electron ledger, and you have the redox definitions used across the
whole course:

- **[[oxidation]] occurs when something loses electrons.**
- **[[reduction]] occurs when something gains electrons.**

The memory hook is **OILRIG**: **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss (of electrons),
**R**eduction **I**s **G**ain (of electrons). Applied to the electrolysis:
Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb is **reduction** — the lead ions gain electrons and are
reduced to lead atoms. 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ is **oxidation** — the bromide ions
lose electrons and are oxidised to bromine molecules. Because one species
losing electrons means another species gaining them, oxidation and reduction
always occur together, and such reactions are called **[[redox]]**
(re**d**uction + **ox**idation). Each half-equation shows only one of the two
processes — hence the name — and in the exam you will be asked to write
**ionic [[half-equation]]s** for the reactions at the electrodes and label each
as oxidation or reduction.

**Other molten substances — the half-equation bank grows.** Electrolyse
molten sodium chloride and you get sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the
anode:

- cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na  *(reduction — sodium ions reduced)*
- anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻  *(oxidation — chloride ions oxidised)*

The 2 in the anode equation is the charge-balance rule in action
(section 4): two 1− ions must shed two electrons to build one Cl₂ molecule,
balancing atoms *and* charge. Molten aluminium oxide gives aluminium at the
cathode and oxygen at the anode. Aluminium sits in Group 3, so it forms 3+
ions, and cancelling a 3+ charge takes three electrons:

- cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al  *(reduction)* — total charge 0 on both sides
  (3+ combined with 3−);
- anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻  *(oxidation)* — each oxide ion carries 2 extra
  electrons, and oxygen atoms pair into O₂, so two ions must shed 4 electrons
  between them.

Molten zinc chloride behaves exactly like its sodium-chloride template:
Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn at the cathode, 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ at the anode. From these
cases come the two generalisations that predict **every** two-element molten
ionic compound: the **metal appears at the cathode** (metals form positive
ions) and the **non-metal at the anode** (non-metals form negative ions); and
**reduction always occurs at the cathode, oxidation always at the anode**.
The mnemonics do this job: **AN OX / RED CAT** — anode oxidation, reduction
cathode. And the ion names from section 2 now earn their origin story:
positive ions are called **[[cation]]s because they are attracted to the
cathode**; negative ions are called **[[anion]]s because they are attracted
to the anode**. Name, electrode, one-to-one.

**The aqueous pivot.** Not every ionic compound can be melted and split: some
decompose before their melting point — copper(II) carbonate breaks into
copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide on gentle heating, so it can never be
electrolysed as a melt. Solutions rescue the situation, but water changes the
game: **when aqueous solutions are electrolysed, the products are not always
the same as when molten salts are.** Water itself is a **[[weak-electrolyte]]** — it ionises very slightly, splitting into hydrogen
ions and hydroxide ions which constantly recombine (the reaction is
reversible). Wherever water is present, those ions compete in the electrolysis
alongside the compound's own ions — and which ion wins the [[discharge]]
competition is decided by the **[[reactivity-series]]**: the more reactive an
element, the greater its tendency to form an ion, and the harder it is to
turn that ion back into an atom. For positive ions, the further down the
reactivity series an element sits, the more easily its ion accepts an
electron.

The apparatus for investigating solution electrolysis (spec 1.60C): an
electrolytic cell — a glass tube fitted with a rubber bung holding two carbon
electrodes — is filled with the solution (concentrated sodium chloride, say),
a small test-tube of the same solution is placed over each electrode (not
fully covering them, or ion flow stops and the current dies), and the
electrodes are wired to a battery or power pack. Bubbles of gas at either
electrode are the sign that something is happening; the gases are collected
and tested. For concentrated sodium chloride solution the results: **hydrogen
at the cathode, chlorine at the anode**. Expect equal volumes in theory but
slightly **less chlorine than expected in practice** — chlorine is more
soluble in water than hydrogen is, so some of it dissolves before it can be
collected (the same solubility quirk, in mirror image, explains section 9's
oxygen shortfall). And chlorine changes everything about the experiment's
handling:

:::safety
Wear eye protection throughout. Chlorine is poisonous — run chlorine-producing
electrolyses in a fume cupboard or well-ventilated room, and do not smell the
products (particularly hazardous for people with asthma). Once chlorine is
detected, switch the current off.
:::

:::exam-hint
Two marks hide in this section that almost every candidate collects.
**Charge-balance check**: after writing any half-equation, add the charges on
both sides — 2O²⁻ (4−) → O₂ + 4e⁻ (4−) balances; an unbalanced total charge
means the electron count is wrong. And the "either equation" courtesy: for
solution electrolyses you may see the hydrogen half-equation written from H⁺
ions (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂) or from water molecules directly (2H₂O + 2e⁻ →
H₂ + 2OH⁻) — both are accepted in answers. The second form earns its keep in
the next section, where it explains why the solution near the cathode turns
alkaline.
:::

:::misconception
"Electrons are lost at the anode, so the anode must be negative — negative
things gain electrons." The sign of an electrode is set by the **power
supply**, not by what lands on it: the supply pulls electrons out of the
anode, making it positive, and anions crawling to it are exactly the species
whose extra electrons it can absorb. Oxidation at a positive electrode sounds
backwards until you separate the two questions — who is short of electrons
(the anode, by construction) and who has electrons to give (the anions, by
charge). AN OX / RED CAT keeps the pairing straight.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.57C/1.58C/1.59C/1.60C items — the OILRIG labels
for the half-equation bank (PbBr₂, NaCl, Al₂O₃, ZnCl₂), the anode/cathode
product generalisation, the cation–cathode/anion–anode naming, and the
solution-electrolysis apparatus. Write the aluminium oxide pair from memory —
it is the charge-balance showcase and examiners know it.
:::

sections.title: The electrolysis of sodium chloride solution
sections.markdown:
Electrolyse **molten** sodium chloride and the products are the ones the
molten rulebook promises: sodium at the cathode, chlorine at the anode.
Electrolyse sodium chloride **solution** and only half the story survives:
**chlorine is still formed at the anode, but hydrogen is produced at the
cathode instead of sodium.** The chlorine comes from the compound's own
chloride ions — but the hydrogen comes from the **water**. That single change
of product is the doorway into every solution electrolysis in this chapter.

Why does water get a vote? Because water is a [[weak-electrolyte]] (section 6):
it ionises very slightly into hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. So the
solution actually contains four ions — Na⁺(aq) and Cl⁻(aq) from the salt,
H⁺(aq) and OH⁻(aq) from the water — and both positive ions arrive at the
cathode together. Which one is [[discharge]]d is decided by the [[reactivity-series]]
rule: **the more reactive the metal, the harder it is to convert its ion back
into an atom.** Sodium is a very reactive metal, so adding an electron to a
Na⁺ ion is extremely difficult; hydrogen is less reactive than sodium, so a
hydrogen ion accepts an electron easily. Hydrogen wins the competition, and
each hydrogen atom formed pairs up with another:

2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g)  *(reduction)*

The hydrogen ions are taken from water molecules splitting up — and each
ionisation that released an H⁺ also released an OH⁻. With the hydrogen ions
being discharged, the hydroxide ions are left accumulating around the
cathode, so **the solution becomes alkaline in the region around that
electrode**. You can see the same story told in a single line by writing the
cathode **[[half-equation]]** straight from water molecules:

2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq)  *(reduction)*

Both forms are accepted in answers; the water form shows the alkalinity
outright because OH⁻ appears as a product.

**At the anode**, chloride ions and hydroxide ions both arrive. The contest
here is close: it is slightly easier to oxidise hydroxide ions than chloride
ions, but there is no great difference — and there are **many, many more
chloride ions** present in a concentrated solution, so it is mainly the
chloride ions that are oxidised to chlorine:

2Cl⁻(aq) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻  *(oxidation)*

Two refinements complete the picture. In a **dilute** sodium chloride
solution, noticeable amounts of **oxygen** appear at the anode alongside the
chlorine, also coming from the hydroxide ions. And the reason every question
stresses [[inert-electrode]]s: the electrode material can change the
products. With **copper** electrodes, oxygen is not produced at the anode at
all — the anode itself gets smaller as the copper goes into solution. Carbon
or platinum electrodes keep the products predictable.

Finally, the long-game question: electrolyse concentrated sodium chloride
solution for a long time and what is left in solution? The ions present were
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (from the salt) and H⁺ and OH⁻ (from the water). Hydrogen ions
and chloride ions are removed from the solution by discharge at the
electrodes. That leaves **Na⁺ and OH⁻ — sodium hydroxide solution**. The
electrolysis of brine, run industrially, makes all three products: hydrogen,
chlorine and sodium hydroxide.

:::key-point
The one-sentence prediction rule this section teaches: **at the cathode, if
the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, hydrogen is produced instead of
the metal.** Sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium and aluminium solutions
all yield hydrogen; copper and the metals below hydrogen yield the metal
itself. The hydrogen always comes from the water — a reminder that the
solvent is a player, not a spectator.
:::

:::exam-hint
The observation marks in this experiment are as bankable as the equations:
hydrogen bubbles at the cathode (tested with a lit splint — squeaky pop),
chlorine at the anode (bleaches damp litmus), and the solution turning
**alkaline near the cathode**. If asked to explain the alkalinity, quote the
water-form half-equation — H⁺ discharged leaves OH⁻ behind — rather than
asserting "sodium hydroxide forms" without the mechanism. And expect the
molten-versus-solution comparison as a two-part question: sodium from the
melt, hydrogen from the solution, same anode product both times.
:::

:::misconception
"Electrolysing sodium chloride solution gives sodium, because the compound
is sodium chloride." The compound's identity decides the **anode** product
(chlorine) but not the cathode one: at the cathode the contest is between
the metal ion and the water's hydrogen ions, and the **more reactive metal
loses** — its ion is too hard to reduce. Sodium's own reactivity, the very
property that makes it a famous metal, is precisely what disqualifies it
here. Hydrogen appears in its place, from water.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.58C/1.59C items — solution-versus-molten products
for sodium chloride, the two cathode half-equation forms, the anode contest,
and the sodium-hydroxide residue. Write both cathode equations and state
which one reveals why the solution goes alkaline.
:::

sections.title: The electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate solution using inert electrodes
sections.markdown:
Copper(II) sulfate solution, CuSO₄(aq), is blue — the colour of its copper
ions — and that colour is the experiment's built-in indicator. The solution
holds four ions: Cu²⁺(aq) and SO₄²⁻(aq) from the salt, H⁺(aq) and OH⁻(aq)
from the water. Run the electrolysis with **inert** (carbon or platinum)
electrodes and watch which ions win each contest.

**At the cathode**, the copper(II) ions and hydrogen ions both arrive.
Copper sits **below hydrogen in the [[reactivity-series]]**, which flips the
sodium case of the last section: an ion of a less reactive metal accepts
electrons easily, so the copper(II) ions are [[discharge]]d in preference to the
hydrogen ions. The cathode becomes coated with **pink-brown copper**:

Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)  *(reduction)*

**At the anode**, sulfate ions and hydroxide ions both arrive — but sulfate
ions are not easy to oxidise at all — they resist [[oxidation]]. The hydroxide ions from the water are
oxidised instead, giving oxygen gas:

4OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) + 4e⁻  *(oxidation)*

As with the sodium chloride cathode, there is an alternative form written
straight from water molecules — and this one reveals what happens to the
solution near the anode:

2H₂O(l) → O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻  *(oxidation)*

Because this equation **produces** hydrogen ions, the solution becomes
**acidic in the region around the anode** — the mirror image of the alkaline
cathode region in the brine experiment.

Now run the electrolysis for a long time and track the colour. The copper
ions are being removed at the cathode and nothing replaces them, so **the
blue colour fades from blue to colourless** as the copper(II) ions are used
up. Then the residue question — what is left in the solution? The ions
originally present were Cu²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ (from the salt) and H⁺ and OH⁻ (from
the water). Copper ions and hydroxide ions are discharged at the electrodes;
hydrogen ions and sulfate ions are not. The leftover ions are H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ —
**the solution has become dilute sulfuric acid**, and from that point the
electrolysis simply continues as the dilute sulfuric acid case of the next
section. The colour-to-colourless fade is the exam's favourite observation
in this experiment; the acid residue is its favourite follow-up.

This experiment doubles as evidence about water itself: collecting hydrogen
at the cathode and oxygen at the anode from solutions where water is the
shared reactant is a classic route to showing that water contains hydrogen
and oxygen — the building blocks of H₂O.

One loose end — what if the dissolved metal is neither above hydrogen like
sodium nor below like copper, but in between, such as **zinc**? For a
moderately reactive metal the answer depends on concentration: reasonably
concentrated solutions give the metal; very dilute solutions give mainly
hydrogen; in between, you get both. The International GCSE keeps its
examples in the clear-cut cases — sodium (hydrogen) and copper (metal) — but
now you know why the rule is a rule about *reactivity*, not an arbitrary
list.

:::key-point
The two-contest summary for copper(II) sulfate solution: **cathode — copper
wins because copper is below hydrogen (less reactive metals' ions reduce
easily)**; anode — hydroxide wins because sulfate refuses to oxidise. Blue
fades to colourless; pink-brown copper builds on the cathode; colourless gas
(oxygen) bubbles at the anode; the final solution is dilute sulfuric acid.
Four observations, four explanations, one reactivity-series rule.
:::

:::exam-hint
This is the observation-to-equation question in its purest form: state what
you would *see* at each electrode (pink-brown coating forming on the cathode;
bubbles of oxygen at the anode; the blue colour fading), then write the
half-equation that explains each observation. Remember the state-symbol
detail in the cathode equation — Cu(s) — because the solid deposit is the
observation. And if the question asks what remains after long electrolysis,
answer in ions first (H⁺ and SO₄²⁻) and only then name the compound (dilute
sulfuric acid): the ionic answer shows the mechanism.
:::

:::misconception
"Copper(II) sulfate solution gives hydrogen at the cathode — all solutions
do." Only solutions of metals **more reactive than hydrogen** surrender the
cathode to hydrogen. Copper is below hydrogen, so its ions are the easy
reduction target and the metal plates out. The reactivity series is the
arbiter in every solution electrolysis: above hydrogen → hydrogen; below
hydrogen → metal. Sodium chloride and copper(II) sulfate, side by side, are
the two exam-standard demonstrations of exactly this split.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.58C/1.59C items — the copper(II) sulfate product
pair, both half-equations, the colour-fade explanation and the acid-residue
argument. Rehearse the four-observation script until each observation calls
up its equation automatically.
:::

sections.title: The electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid using inert electrodes
sections.markdown:
Dilute sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄(aq), strips the contest down to its simplest
form. The solution's ions: H⁺(aq) and SO₄²⁻(aq) from the acid, plus H⁺(aq)
and OH⁻(aq) from the water. At the cathode the only positive ions arriving
are hydrogen ions — from both the acid and the water — so there is no
competition at all: they are [[discharge]]d directly, pairing into molecules as
they form:

2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g)  *(reduction)*

At the anode the sulfate ions arrive with the hydroxide ions, and exactly as
in the copper(II) sulfate experiment, the sulfate ions are too difficult to
oxidise. The hydroxide ions from the water give up their extra electrons
instead, yielding oxygen:

4OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g) + 4e⁻  *(oxidation)*

So dilute sulfuric acid electrolysis is really the **electrolysis of water**,
with the acid's role being to carry the current: **hydrogen at the cathode,
oxygen at the anode, and nothing consumed but water.**

The volume story is the part examiners examine. Read the two
**[[half-equation]]s** as an electron ledger: every 4 electrons flowing round the circuit buy
**1 molecule of O₂** at the anode — but the same 4 electrons would have
produced **2 molecules of H₂** at the cathode (each H₂ molecule costing 2
electrons). Twice the molecules, twice the volume: **twice as much hydrogen
is produced as oxygen.** Equal numbers of gas molecules occupy equal volumes
at the same temperature and pressure, so the ratio of the equations carries
straight through to the gas syringes.

Reality adds one honest footnote: when the experiment is actually done, the
hydrogen collected is **more than twice** the oxygen. Oxygen is slightly
more soluble in water than hydrogen, so a little of it dissolves away before
it can be collected. The standard fix is procedural, and describing it earns
its mark: run the electrolysis for a few minutes **before** starting to
collect, letting the water become saturated with dissolved oxygen — then
collect the gases, and the measured ratio improves dramatically.

:::key-point
The 2 : 1 ratio is a half-equation argument, not a memory item: 4 electrons
→ 2H₂ (cathode) but only 1O₂ (anode), and equal molecule counts mean equal
volumes for gases. Whenever a question asks "explain why twice as much
hydrogen is produced", the answer is the electron arithmetic of these two
half-equations — never "hydrogen is lighter" or any density-flavoured
guess.
:::

:::exam-hint
Expect three question shapes here. (1) *Predict the products*: hydrogen and
oxygen — the "no contest" electrolysis, since the only positive ion is H⁺
and sulfate refuses to oxidise. (2) *Explain the 2 : 1 volume ratio* from
the half-equations. (3) *Why is the measured ratio wrong, and how do you
fix it?* — oxygen's solubility, and pre-saturating the water by running the
electrolysis before collecting. The apparatus for measuring the volumes is
the gas-syringe or measuring-cylinder-over-electrode setup, and it returns
in the next section doing quantitative work.
:::

:::misconception
"Electrolysing sulfuric acid must give sulfur, because sulfate ions contain
sulfur." Sulfate ions are never discharged in these experiments — they are
too difficult to oxidise, which is precisely why the water's hydroxide ions
do the anode work. Nothing sulfur-flavoured appears at either electrode: the
acid's hydrogen ions join the water's at the cathode, its sulfate ions sit
in the solution unused, and both products come from water. The same logic
saw off "sulfur at the cathode" in the copper(II) sulfate residue question.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.58C/1.59C items — the products of dilute sulfuric
acid electrolysis, both half-equations, and the 2 : 1 volume-ratio argument.
Produce the electron-ledger explanation in two sentences from memory; it is
the model answer for every "explain the volumes" question in this topic.
:::

sections.title: The electrolysis of some other solutions — and the quantitative close
sections.markdown:
Every solution electrolysis of the last three sections was one instance of
two rules, and stated plainly, the rules predict **any** solution the exam
can name (spec 1.58C):

- **Cathode (−):** if the metal is **high in the [[reactivity-series]]** (above
  hydrogen), **hydrogen** is produced instead of the metal; if the metal is
  **below hydrogen**, **the metal itself** is produced.
- **Anode (+):** for solutions of **halides** — chlorides, bromides,
  iodides — the **halogen** (chlorine, bromine or iodine) is produced; for
  solutions of other common negative ions — **sulfate, nitrate, hydroxide**
  — **oxygen** is produced (from the water's hydroxide ions).

The rulebook at work, one table, four solutions with inert (carbon or
platinum) electrodes:

| Solution | Cathode product | Cathode half-equation | Anode product | Anode half-equation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KI(aq) | hydrogen | 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ | iodine | 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ |
| MgBr₂(aq) | hydrogen | 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ | bromine | 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ |
| H₂SO₄(aq) | hydrogen | 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ | oxygen | 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻ |
| CuSO₄(aq) | copper | Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu | oxygen | 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻ |

Check each row against the rules: potassium and magnesium sit above hydrogen
(hydrogen wins the cathode); copper sits below (copper wins); iodide and
bromide are halides (halogen at the anode); sulfate is not (oxygen at the
anode). Two honest exceptions to keep in view: the covalent substances that
*do* conduct in solution because they ionise in water — the **acids and
ammonia solution** — and the reason every question hammers the word
**inert**. For electrolysis to work at all, **ions must be present** and free
to move: the external circuit can carry current only if the [[electrolyte]]
completes it. Electrolyse a covalent molecular substance such as sugar
solution (or molten sugar) and nothing happens — no ions, no current, no
decomposition. Sugar is a **[[non-electrolyte]]**. Flip that logic and you
own a diagnostic: **if a substance undergoes electrolysis, molten or in
solution, it must contain ions; if it does not, it has none.** Electrolysis
is itself the test for ionic character.

**The quantitative experiment (spec 1.60C).** "How much?" can be measured:
electrolysis products are produced in amounts that depend on the current, and
the experiment that shows it is a planning favourite. The apparatus extends
the solution-electrolysis cell with three measuring instruments — a
**variable resistor** to set the current, an **ammeter** to read it, and a
**gas burette** (or measuring cylinder) over the cathode to collect and
measure the hydrogen. The procedure, as a variables-and-controls script:

- pour 50 cm³ of concentrated sodium chloride solution into the cell and
  place the gas burette over the cathode;
- switch on and **set the current to 0.2 A with the variable resistor**
  (reading taken from the ammeter — the current must be flowing before the
  burette can be read, so the initial burette reading is taken after
  switching on);
- run for **5 minutes** (timed), then record the volume of hydrogen
  collected;
- **repeat for currents of 0.4 A, 0.6 A, 0.8 A and 1.0 A** — the independent
  variable is the current, the dependent variable the gas volume, and the
  controlled variables include the solution volume and concentration and the
  electrolysis time;
- **repeat each experiment** and average, to improve reliability.

A representative set of results:

| Current / A | Volume of hydrogen / cm³ |
|---|---|
| 0.2 | 7.0 |
| 0.4 | 13.9 |
| 0.6 | 15.1 |
| 0.8 | 28.0 |
| 1.0 | 34.9 |

Current is continuous data, so the graph is drawn as a **line of best fit**
— and here sits the analysis skill the examiner wants: the 0.6 A reading of
15.1 cm³ is **anomalous** (too low; the current may have dipped or some gas
escaped), so it is **excluded when drawing the line of best fit**. The
remaining points sit on a straight line **through the origin**, and a
straight line through the origin is the signature of a **directly
proportional** relationship: **the volume of gas produced is directly
proportional to the current passed.** Bigger current, more electrons per
second, more product — the chemistry's electron ledger made visible in a
graph.

:::summary
Electrolysis is the chemical change caused by passing a current through a
molten compound or solution — possible only where ions are free to move, and
driven at two electrodes: the **positive anode**, where anions are
discharged and **oxidation** happens, and the **negative cathode**, where
cations are discharged and **reduction** happens (OILRIG; AN OX / RED CAT).
Molten two-element compounds split into metal at the cathode and non-metal
at the anode, each event written as a charge-balanced ionic half-equation.
In solution, water joins as a weak electrolyte and the reactivity series
decides: above hydrogen → hydrogen at the cathode; below → the metal;
halides → halogen at the anode, other ions → oxygen. The products obey a
measurable law: gas volume directly proportional to current — electrolysis
as electron bookkeeping made visible.
:::

:::can-you
- State the two conditions for conduction and name the mobile particle in
  each of the three structure types?
- Define *electrolysis*, *electrolyte*, *electrode*, *anode*, *cathode*,
  *anion* and *cation* — and explain where the ion names come from?
- Describe the molten lead(II) bromide experiment with all four observations
  and both half-equations, labelled?
- Write and balance the half-equations for molten NaCl, Al₂O₃ and ZnCl₂,
  and say why the electron counts differ?
- Predict the products for any named solution — NaCl, CuSO₄, dilute H₂SO₄,
  KI, MgBr₂ — and justify each prediction from the two rules?
- Explain why sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen (both half-equation
  forms) and why the blue colour of copper(II) sulfate fades?
- Account for the 2 : 1 hydrogen-to-oxygen volume ratio in dilute sulfuric
  acid electrolysis — and why reality over-delivers on the hydrogen?
- Describe the quantitative experiment (variables, method) and read a
  proportional graph, anomalies included?
:::

:::cross-curricular
Electrolysis is one of the load-bearing processes of modern industry. The
aluminium in aircraft and drink cans is won from its ore by molten electrolysis
— chemical reduction cannot manage it, and the lesson's Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al
half-equation is the industrial reaction, run at enormous scale. The brine
electrolysis of section 7 supplies chlorine for water treatment and plastics,
hydrogen for the chemical industry, and sodium hydroxide for soap — three
products, one cell. Electroplating uses the copper-style cathode deposition to
coat objects with metal. And the quantitative law you plotted — product
amount proportional to current — is the working rule every electroplater and
chlorine plant operator sets their dials by.
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection. Where chlorine is produced (concentrated chloride
solutions), work in a fume cupboard or well-ventilated room, do not smell the
gas — a particular hazard for people with asthma — and switch the current off
as soon as chlorine is detected.
:::

:::exam-hint
The graph question is where this chapter quietly examines experimental
skills: name the anomaly, justify excluding it from the line of best fit,
state the proportional conclusion, and — the top mark — connect the physics
to the chemistry (more current = more electrons per second = more product,
because each product molecule costs a fixed number of electrons). When
predicting unfamiliar products, quote the rules *and* the ionic contest they
summarise; the rule earns the mark, the contest explains it if the question
pushes to "why".
:::

:::misconception
"The anomalous 0.6 A point should be joined up with the others — excluding
data sounds like cheating." Discarding an anomaly from a line of best fit is
not dishonesty; it is the standard treatment of a known bad reading, provided
you say so. The line of best fit describes the *trend* supported by the
reliable points; one suspect reading (15.1 cm³ when the trend says roughly
21 cm³) would drag the line off and hide the proportionality that four other
points agree on. The dishonest options are the other two: keeping the point
and faking the line, or deleting the reading without declaring it.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.58C/1.60C items — the prediction-rule table across
unfamiliar solutions, the non-electrolyte diagnostic, and the quantitative
experiment's variables, anomaly handling and proportionality conclusion. If
you can fill in the four-row table from the rules alone and sketch the
graph with its annotated anomaly, this chapter — and Unit 1 — is complete.
:::
